moduleTitle: God as Creator: God in and through the universe, and separate from it

note.specFocus: Spec 3.1.7.1 Key beliefs: God as Creator, including different aspects of God's relationship with creation – God shown in and through the universe; God as separate from the universe.
note.summary:
God as Karta Purakh (Creator) is one of the first ideas in the Mool Mantra. Sikhs believe that God created the universe out of God's own will, without using any pre-existing material, and continues to sustain it.

HOW GOD CREATED
• Before creation, there was only God. Guru Nanak's Maru Solhe (Ang 1035) describes 'endless ages of utter darkness' with no earth, sky, day, night, sun or moon – only God's hukam (command) and God in deep meditation (sunn samadh).
• God then created by a single word: 'You created the vast expanse of the universe with One Word, and hundreds of thousands of rivers began to flow' (Japji pauri 16, Ang 3).
• Only God knows when creation happened (Japji pauri 21, Ang 4). The Guru Granth Sahib describes countless worlds, skies and galaxies (Japji pauri 22, Ang 5), which many Sikhs see as consistent with modern science.
• God can also bring creation back into God's self; creation and dissolution happen in cycles according to hukam.

TWO ASPECTS OF GOD'S RELATIONSHIP WITH CREATION
1. God shown in and through the universe – IMMANENT, sometimes called SARGUN ('with qualities'). God's light (jot) is in every part of creation: 'Among all is the Light – You are that Light' (Ang 13). Guru Nanak wrote 'I am a sacrifice to Your creation (kudrat); You are pervading it' (Ang 469). So nature and people reveal God.
2. God as separate from the universe – TRANSCENDENT, NIRGUN ('without qualities'). God existed before creation, is beyond time (Akal) and space, and cannot be contained or fully described by anything created. God is not the same as the universe.
Sikhs hold both together: God is in everything but also infinitely greater than everything. This is sometimes compared to an artist present in a painting but not limited to it.

CONSEQUENCES FOR SIKH LIFE
• Respect for nature – environmental care is a religious duty. EcoSikh and Sikh Environment Day (14 March, linked to Guru Har Rai's love of nature) encourage tree-planting and green gurdwaras.
• Respect for all people, since God's light is in all.
• Humility and gratitude, and acceptance of hukam – God's order.
• Maya: the created world is real but temporary; attachment to it (moh) is a barrier to mukti.

DIVERSITY OF VIEW
Most Sikhs see science (Big Bang, evolution) as compatible with gurbani; a few interpret scripture more literally. Some Sikhs emphasise the nirgun God of meditation, others the sargun God seen in the Gurus' teaching and nature. Atheists and humanists argue science explains the universe without God.

KEY TERMS: Karta Purakh, hukam, kudrat, jot, sargun, nirgun, immanent, transcendent, maya, Ang.

questions.question:
Which one of the following Punjabi words refers to God's creation or the natural world?
A Kudrat
B Haumai
C Hukam
D Mukti
questions.modelAnswer: A – Kudrat. Kudrat means nature/creation, in which God's creative power is seen. Haumai is ego, hukam is God's will or command, and mukti is liberation.
evidence: Asa di Var, Ang 469 – 'Balihari kudrat vasia'
questions.examTip: Read all four options before choosing. Only one is correct; write the letter clearly. If unsure, cross out options you know are wrong first.

questions.question:
Which one of the following best describes the Sikh belief that God is both within creation and beyond it?
A God is only found in the gurdwara
B God is immanent and transcendent
C God created the world and then left it alone
D God is identical to the physical universe and nothing more
questions.modelAnswer: B – God is immanent and transcendent. Sikhs believe God is present in and through the universe (sargun) and also separate from and greater than it (nirgun). C and D each describe only half of this belief, and A wrongly limits God to one place.
questions.examTip: Read all four options before choosing. Only one is correct; write the letter clearly. If unsure, cross out options you know are wrong first.

questions.question: Give one Sikh belief about how God created the universe.
questions.modelAnswer: Any one of: God created by a single word/command (hukam) – 'You created the vast expanse with One Word' (Japji, Ang 3); before creation there was only darkness and God alone in deep meditation (Ang 1035); God created out of God's own will; creation came from God, not from pre-existing matter.
questions.examTip: A 1-mark short response needs one accurate, relevant point only. A short phrase or sentence is enough; do not waste time explaining.

questions.question: Give one meaning of the term 'nirgun'.
questions.modelAnswer: God without attributes/qualities – God as transcendent, beyond and separate from creation and beyond human understanding.
questions.examTip: A 1-mark short response needs one accurate, relevant point only. A short phrase or sentence is enough; do not waste time explaining.

questions.question: Explain two ways in which the belief that God is present in creation influences Sikhs today.
questions.modelAnswer:
First way: Sikhs respect and care for the environment. Because God's light is in all of nature (kudrat), harming the earth is seen as disrespecting God. For example, the EcoSikh movement encourages gurdwaras to plant trees and reduce waste, and Sikhs mark Sikh Environment Day each March.

Second way: Sikhs respect all people. If God is present in every person, then every human deserves dignity, whatever their religion, caste or gender. This leads Sikhs to serve everyone in the langar and to see sewa to others as serving God.
evidence: Ang 13 – 'Sabh meh jot jot hai soi'
questions.examTip: Give two separate ways. For each, make a simple point (1 mark) and then develop it with an example, consequence or detail (2 marks). Two undeveloped points score only 2.

questions.question: Explain two ways in which belief in God as Creator influences Sikhs today.
questions.modelAnswer:
First way: It makes Sikhs humble and grateful. Since everything they have – life, family, wealth – was created and given by God, Sikhs thank God in daily prayer (for example in Ardas) and try not to become proud, which helps them overcome haumai.

Second way: It encourages Sikhs to accept God's will (hukam). If God created and sustains everything, then events in life happen within God's order. Many Sikhs try to respond calmly to difficulties, echoing Guru Arjan's words 'Tera keea meetha laagai' ('Your actions seem sweet to me'), rather than blaming God.

questions.question:
Explain two Sikh teachings about God's relationship with creation.
Refer to sacred writings or another source of Sikh belief and teaching in your answer.
questions.modelAnswer:
First teaching: God is shown in and through the universe (immanent, sargun). God's light is in every part of creation and in every person, so the world itself reveals God. Sikhs may say they see God's hand in the beauty and order of nature.

Second teaching: God is also separate from the universe (transcendent, nirgun). God existed before creation, in deep meditation in the void, and is not limited by space or time. God is beyond the universe and cannot be fully described by any created thing.

Source: In Asa di Var Guru Nanak writes 'I am a sacrifice to Your creation; You are pervading it' (Ang 469), showing God is in creation. The Maru Solhe hymn on Ang 1035 says that for countless ages there was only darkness and God alone, showing God existed independently before and apart from creation.
questions.examTip: Explain two teachings, each developed (2 + 2 marks), then name a source of Sikh authority AND apply it to the question (2 marks). Naming the Guru Granth Sahib with an Ang number, or a Guru's teaching, and showing how it supports your point is the safest way to get the source marks.

questions.question:
Explain two Sikh beliefs about the creation of the universe.
Refer to sacred writings or another source of Sikh belief and teaching in your answer.
questions.modelAnswer:
First belief: The universe was created by God's word or command (hukam). God did not need materials or helpers; the whole universe came into existence because God willed it. This shows God's total power as Karta Purakh.

Second belief: Before creation there was only God in a state of formless meditation, with no earth, sky, day or night. God then chose to create, and creation is continuous – God sustains it at every moment and can draw it back again. This is compatible, for many Sikhs, with scientific ideas such as the Big Bang.

Source: Japji Sahib, pauri 16 (Ang 3) says 'You created the vast expanse of the universe with One Word', applying the idea that creation came from God's command. Guru Nanak's Maru Solhe (Ang 1035) describes the darkness before creation, when there was only God's command (hukam).
evidence: Japji pauri 16, Ang 3 – 'Keeta pasao eko kavao'

Naming the Guru Granth Sahib with an Ang number, or a Guru's teaching, and showing how it supports your point is the safest way to get the source marks.

questions.question:
“God is easier to find in nature than in a gurdwara.”
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• refer to Sikh teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
ARGUMENTS IN SUPPORT

Sikhs believe God is shown in and through the universe. Guru Nanak praised God's presence in kudrat (creation) – 'I am a sacrifice to Your creation; You are pervading it' (Ang 469). A sunrise, a mountain or a living creature can make a person aware of God's power and beauty directly, without any building.

The Guru Granth Sahib often uses images of nature – rivers, the ocean, the lotus, the moth and flame – to describe God. Guru Nanak himself travelled widely (the udasis) and taught in open places as well as homes. His hymn 'Gagan mai thaal' (Ang 13) describes the whole universe as a natural arti (worship) to God, suggesting nature itself worships God.

Some people find buildings and rituals distracting or divisive, and feel closer to God when alone in nature. Many non-religious people also say nature gives them a sense of awe, even if they do not call it God.

ARGUMENTS FOR A DIFFERENT VIEW

God is also transcendent (nirgun) – beyond nature. Nature shows God's creation, but not God's full reality, and enjoying nature can become maya (illusion) and attachment if it is not linked to remembering God's Name. Sikhs believe God is found through the Guru's grace (Gurprasad), and the Guru today is the Guru Granth Sahib, which is housed in the gurdwara.

In the gurdwara Sikhs hear gurbani and kirtan, join the sangat and take part in langar. The Guru Granth Sahib says the true company (satsangat) is where the One Name is spoken (Ang 72). The sangat supports people to become gurmukh, which is harder alone in nature.

Sikhs also teach that God is found within, by meditating on the Name (nam japna). The place matters less than the state of the mind: someone can walk in a forest full of haumai, or sit in a gurdwara and be truly focused on God.

CONCLUSION

Nature certainly reveals God for Sikhs, because God pervades creation. But Sikhism teaches that God is most fully known through the Guru's word and the Name, which the gurdwara makes available through the Guru Granth Sahib and the sangat. So it is not 'easier' to find God in nature; rather, nature and the gurdwara work together, and for Sikhs the deciding factor is an inward, God-centred mind.

questions.question:
“Science has replaced the need for a Creator God.”
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• refer to Sikh teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
ARGUMENTS IN SUPPORT

Many atheists and humanists argue that science gives a complete explanation of how the universe came about. The Big Bang theory explains the origin of the universe around 13.8 billion years ago and evolution explains the development of life, so there is no need to bring in God as Karta Purakh.

Scientific explanations are based on evidence that can be tested, whereas religious beliefs about creation rely on revelation. On this view, belief in a Creator was useful before people understood nature, but is now unnecessary.

ARGUMENTS FOR A DIFFERENT VIEW

Most Sikhs see no conflict between science and the Guru Granth Sahib. The scripture describes a vast universe with 'hundreds of thousands of nether worlds and skies' (Japji pauri 22, Ang 5) and countless galaxies, which many Sikhs say fits modern astronomy. Guru Nanak's description of a time of only darkness before creation (Ang 1035) is often compared to the state before the Big Bang.

Sikhs believe God created by a single command: 'You created the vast expanse with One Word' (Ang 3). Science explains how the universe developed, but Sikhs argue it cannot explain why there is anything at all, or why the universe has order. God's hukam is the reason behind the laws that science describes.

Sikhs also believe the purpose of creation is spiritual – human life is a chance to unite with God (Ang 12). Science does not answer questions of meaning or purpose, so the need for God remains. The Guru Granth Sahib even says that only the Creator knows when creation happened (Japji pauri 21, Ang 4), showing humility about how much humans can know.

CONCLUSION

Science has replaced some older literal ideas about how the world began, but it has not replaced the need for a Creator for those who ask why the universe exists and what life is for. Sikhism is well placed here, because its scripture already describes an immense, evolving universe ruled by God's order. The stronger view is that science and belief in a Creator answer different questions, so science has not removed the need for God.
